India first joined the [Olympic Games](https://kids.kiddle.co/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") in 1900. This made India the first country from Asia to take part! A single athlete, [Norman Pritchard](https://kids.kiddle.co/Norman_Pritchard "Norman Pritchard"), represented India. He won two silver medals in [athletics](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sport_of_athletics "Sport of athletics").

India sent its first team to the [Summer Olympic Games](https://kids.kiddle.co/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games") in 1920. Since then, India has been part of every Summer Games. India also started competing in the [Winter Olympic Games](https://kids.kiddle.co/Winter_Olympic_Games "Winter Olympic Games") in 1964.

Indian athletes have won 41 medals so far, all at the Summer Games. For many years, the Indian Men's Field Hockey Team was super strong in the Olympics. They won eleven medals between 1928 and 1980. This included eight gold medals, with six of them won in a row from 1928 to 1956! India had its best performance ever at the 2020 Games. They won seven medals, including one gold and two silver medals.

## India's Olympic Journey

### Early Days Before Independence

[![Image 5: India hockey team 1928](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/8/81/India_hockey_team_1928.jpg/300px-India_hockey_team_1928.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:India_hockey_team_1928.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:India_hockey_team_1928.jpg "Enlarge")

 Indian field hockey team that won the gold medal at the 1928 Olympics

India's first time at the Olympics was in 1900. Back then, India was part of [British India](https://kids.kiddle.co/British_Raj "British Raj"). As mentioned, it was the first Asian country to join the Games. [Norman Pritchard](https://kids.kiddle.co/Norman_Pritchard "Norman Pritchard") was the only athlete from India. He won two silver medals in athletics. India ranked 19th in medals that year, which is still its best rank ever!

India did not compete in the next three Summer Olympics. Then, in 1920, a businessman named Dorabji Tata helped India get a spot on the [International Olympic Committee](https://kids.kiddle.co/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee"). This allowed India to compete on its own at the 1920 Summer Olympics. India sent six athletes, including four runners and two [wrestlers](https://kids.kiddle.co/Wrestling_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Wrestling at the Summer Olympics").

The Indian Olympic movement grew in the 1920s. In 1927, the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) was officially recognized. This group helps develop sports in India and picks teams for the Olympics. For the [1928 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1928_Summer_Olympics "1928 Summer Olympics") in [Amsterdam](https://kids.kiddle.co/Amsterdam "Amsterdam"), India sent eight athletes. The Indian Hockey Federation also sent the men's hockey team. This team won India's first ever Olympic gold medal in Amsterdam! It was also the first gold medal won by any Asian country in the modern Olympics.

[![Image 6: Indian-Hockey-Team-Berlin-1936](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/8/8e/Indian-Hockey-Team-Berlin-1936.jpg/300px-Indian-Hockey-Team-Berlin-1936.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Indian-Hockey-Team-Berlin-1936.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Indian-Hockey-Team-Berlin-1936.jpg "Enlarge")

 Indian hockey team at the 1936 Berlin Olympics

The Indian hockey team continued its winning streak. They won three gold medals in a row from 1928 to 1936. In 1932, they beat the United States 24–1, which is the biggest win in Olympic history! In the 1936 final, they beat Germany 8–1.

### After India Became Independent

[![Image 7: Hockey Nederland India. Elftal India, Bestanddeelnr 902-9315](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/5/52/Hockey_Nederland_India._Elftal_India%2C_Bestanddeelnr_902-9315.jpg/300px-Hockey_Nederland_India._Elftal_India%2C_Bestanddeelnr_902-9315.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Hockey_Nederland_India._Elftal_India,_Bestanddeelnr_902-9315.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Hockey_Nederland_India._Elftal_India,_Bestanddeelnr_902-9315.jpg "Enlarge")

 Indian field hockey team that won the first gold medal after independence at the 1948 London Olympics

India became an independent country in 1947. It sent its first team as an independent nation to the [1948 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1948_Summer_Olympics "1948 Summer Olympics") in [London](https://kids.kiddle.co/London "London"). India sent 79 athletes who competed in ten sports. This included India's first time in arts, [boxing](https://kids.kiddle.co/Boxing_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Boxing at the Summer Olympics"), [cycling](https://kids.kiddle.co/Cycling_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Cycling at the Summer Olympics"), [football](https://kids.kiddle.co/Football_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Football at the Summer Olympics"), and [water polo](https://kids.kiddle.co/Water_polo_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Water polo at the Summer Olympics"). The Indian field hockey team won the only medal, a gold. This was India's first medal as an independent country.

The [1952 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1952_Summer_Olympics "1952 Summer Olympics") were special because India sent women competitors for the first time. The team had 64 athletes, including four women. Wrestler K. D. Jadhav won a bronze medal. This was the first individual medal for independent India. The Indian field hockey team won its sixth straight gold medal in 1956. In the [1960 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1960_Summer_Olympics "1960 Summer Olympics") in [Rome](https://kids.kiddle.co/Rome "Rome"), the hockey team won a silver medal after losing to Pakistan. This was their first loss in the Olympics since 1928.

India first competed in the [Winter Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/Winter_Olympic_Games "Winter Olympic Games") in [1964](https://kids.kiddle.co/1964_Winter_Olympics "1964 Winter Olympics") in [Innsbruck](https://kids.kiddle.co/Innsbruck "Innsbruck"). Jeremy Bujakowski competed in [alpine skiing](https://kids.kiddle.co/Alpine_skiing_at_the_Winter_Olympics "Alpine skiing at the Winter Olympics"). Later that year, at the [1964 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1964_Summer_Olympics "1964 Summer Olympics") in [Tokyo](https://kids.kiddle.co/Tokyo "Tokyo"), the men's field hockey team won another gold medal. This was India's only medal at those Games.

[![Image 8: Paes US16 (11) (29569576630)](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/b/bd/Paes_US16_%2811%29_%2829569576630%29.jpg/230px-Paes_US16_%2811%29_%2829569576630%29.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Paes_US16_(11)_(29569576630).jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Paes_US16_(11)_(29569576630).jpg "Enlarge")

[Leander Paes](https://kids.kiddle.co/Leander_Paes "Leander Paes") won a bronze medal in 1996. This was India's first Olympic medal in almost 16 years.

India sent its smallest team since independence to the [1968 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1968_Summer_Olympics "1968 Summer Olympics") in [Mexico City](https://kids.kiddle.co/Mexico_City "Mexico City"). India did not compete in the Winter Olympics from 1972 to 1984. In the [1972 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1972_Summer_Olympics "1972 Summer Olympics") in [Munich](https://kids.kiddle.co/Munich "Munich"), the men's field hockey team won a bronze medal. In [1976 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1976_Summer_Olympics "1976 Summer Olympics") in [Montreal](https://kids.kiddle.co/Montreal "Montreal"), India did not win any medals. This was the first time since 1924.

At the [1980 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1980_Summer_Olympics "1980 Summer Olympics") in [Moscow](https://kids.kiddle.co/Moscow "Moscow"), the men's hockey team won their eighth Olympic gold medal. This was their last gold medal in hockey at the Olympics. India did not win any medals in the next three Summer Olympics (1984, 1988, 1992). India returned to the Winter Olympics in [1988](https://kids.kiddle.co/1988_Winter_Olympics "1988 Winter Olympics"). The team included the first Indian woman participant, Shailaja Kumar. In 1996, tennis player [Leander Paes](https://kids.kiddle.co/Leander_Paes "Leander Paes") won a bronze medal. This was India's first Olympic medal in almost 16 years! He was also the first Indian individual medalist since 1952.

### India in the 21st Century

[![Image 9: Olympic Freestyle Wrestling (66 kg - Medalists)](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/8/86/Olympic_Freestyle_Wrestling_%2866_kg_-_Medalists%29.jpg/300px-Olympic_Freestyle_Wrestling_%2866_kg_-_Medalists%29.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Olympic_Freestyle_Wrestling_(66_kg_-_Medalists).jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Olympic_Freestyle_Wrestling_(66_kg_-_Medalists).jpg "Enlarge")

[Sushil Kumar](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sushil_Kumar "Sushil Kumar") (left) was the first Indian athlete to win more than one individual Olympic medal after independence.

At the [2000 Sydney Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/2000_Summer_Olympics "2000 Summer Olympics"), [Karnam Malleswari](https://kids.kiddle.co/Karnam_Malleswari "Karnam Malleswari") won a bronze medal in weightlifting. This was the first-ever Olympic medal won by an Indian woman! In 2004, shooter [Rajyavardhan Singh Rathore](https://kids.kiddle.co/Rajyavardhan_Singh_Rathore "Rajyavardhan Singh Rathore") won a silver medal.

The [2008 Beijing Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") was a great success for India. The country won three medals, including one gold and two bronze. [Abhinav Bindra](https://kids.kiddle.co/Abhinav_Bindra "Abhinav Bindra") became the first Indian to win an individual gold medal! He won in men's air rifle. [Vijender Singh](https://kids.kiddle.co/Vijender_Singh "Vijender Singh") won India's first Olympic medal in boxing. [Sushil Kumar](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sushil_Kumar "Sushil Kumar") won a bronze in wrestling.

The [2012 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics") saw India win its highest number of medals at the time: six medals (two silver and four bronze). Sushil Kumar won a silver medal, becoming the first Indian since independence to win multiple individual Olympic medals. Shooter Vijay Kumar won another silver. [Saina Nehwal](https://kids.kiddle.co/Saina_Nehwal "Saina Nehwal") won India's first medal in badminton. Boxer [Mary Kom](https://kids.kiddle.co/Mary_Kom "Mary Kom") became the first Indian woman to win a medal in boxing.

[![Image 10: Mary Kom with young sportsperson](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/a/a4/Mary_Kom_with_young_sportsperson.jpg/300px-Mary_Kom_with_young_sportsperson.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Mary_Kom_with_young_sportsperson.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Mary_Kom_with_young_sportsperson.jpg "Enlarge")

[Mary Kom](https://kids.kiddle.co/Mary_Kom "Mary Kom") won India's first medal in women's boxing at the [2012 Games](https://kids.kiddle.co/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics").

In 2014, the Indian Olympic Association was temporarily suspended. This meant some Indian athletes competed as independent participants at the [2014 Winter Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/2014_Winter_Olympics "2014 Winter Olympics"). But the suspension was lifted during the Games, and two athletes then competed under the Indian flag.

For the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics"), India sent over 100 athletes for the first time. India won two medals: one silver and one bronze. Shuttler [P. V. Sindhu](https://kids.kiddle.co/P._V._Sindhu "P. V. Sindhu") won a silver medal, becoming the first Indian woman to win an Olympic silver. Sakshi Malik became the first Indian female wrestler to win an Olympic medal, earning a bronze.

[![Image 11: Neeraj Chopra Olympic gold medalist](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/f/fb/Neeraj_Chopra_Olympic_gold_medalist.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Neeraj_Chopra_Olympic_gold_medalist.jpg)

# China at the Olympics facts for kids

[Kids Encyclopedia Facts](https://kids.kiddle.co/)

This page is about the team organized by the People's Republic of China and represents "China" to compete in the Olympics. For the team organized by the Republic of China to compete in the Olympics from 1924 to 1948, see Republic of China at the Olympics. For the team now representing the Republic of China on Taiwan, see [Chinese Taipei at the Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/Chinese_Taipei_at_the_Olympics "Chinese Taipei at the Olympics"). For the Olympics in China, see Chinese Olympics.

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Number_of_medals_won_by_China_at_Olympic_summer_games_from_1952_to_2012.png "Enlarge")

[![Image 6: Number of medals won by China at Olympic winter games from 1980 to 2012](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/1/1a/Number_of_medals_won_by_China_at_Olympic_winter_games_from_1980_to_2012.png/300px-Number_of_medals_won_by_China_at_Olympic_winter_games_from_1980_to_2012.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Number_of_medals_won_by_China_at_Olympic_winter_games_from_1980_to_2012.png)

 Number of medals won by China at the Olympic Winter Games from 1980 to 2022

China first joined the [Olympic Games](https://kids.kiddle.co/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") as the Republic of China (ROC) from 1924 to 1948. Later, the [People's Republic of China](https://kids.kiddle.co/People%27s_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") (PRC) competed for the first time at the [1952 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1952_Summer_Olympics "1952 Summer Olympics") in Helsinki, Finland. They arrived late but managed to take part in one event.

At that time, the [International Olympic Committee](https://kids.kiddle.co/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") (IOC) allowed both the PRC and ROC (which had moved to Taiwan) to use the name "China." However, the ROC team left in protest. This led to a period where the PRC did not join many international sports events.

China officially returned to the IOC in 1979. This allowed them to send a team to the [1980 Winter Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1980_Winter_Olympics "1980 Winter Olympics") in Lake Placid, USA. Their first time back at the [Summer Olympic Games](https://kids.kiddle.co/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games") after 1952 was the [1984 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics") in Los Angeles, USA.

As of 2024, China has done very well in the Summer Olympics. They finished first once, second four times, and third twice. China is the most successful country in the [Asia](https://kids.kiddle.co/Asia "Asia")–[Oceania](https://kids.kiddle.co/Oceania "Oceania") region. They are the 3rd most successful country in Olympic history, after the United States and the Soviet Union.

The Chinese Olympic Committee was officially recognized in 1979. Before the [Chinese Civil War](https://kids.kiddle.co/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War"), athletes from China competed as the Republic of China (ROC). After the war, the ROC continued to compete, but only with athletes from Taiwan. This was from the 1952 Summer Olympics to the 1976 Winter Olympics.

Because of arguments over the name "China," the PRC boycotted the Games during these years. In 1979, the IOC helped both sides agree. The "China" name would be used by the People's Republic of China. The Republic of China, based in Taipei, would be called _[Chinese Taipei](https://kids.kiddle.co/Chinese\_Taipei\_at\_the\_Olympics "Chinese Taipei at the Olympics")_. This agreement allowed the PRC to finally join the Olympic movement again.

[Hong Kong](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hong_Kong_at_the_Olympics "Hong Kong at the Olympics") has had its own Olympic Committee since 1950. It has competed in the Games separately since 1952. Even after Hong Kong became part of the PRC in 1997, it still competes on its own as _Hong Kong, China_.

## Hosting the Olympic Games

China has hosted the Olympic Games two times. Both times, the host city was [Beijing](https://kids.kiddle.co/Beijing "Beijing"). Beijing is special because it is the first city to host both the Summer and Winter Olympics.

### Olympic Games Hosted by China

| Games | Host City | Dates | Nations | Participants | Events |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [2008 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") | Beijing | August 8–24 | 204 | 10,942 | 302 |
| [2022 Winter Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/2022_Winter_Olympics "2022 Winter Olympics") | Beijing | February 4–20 | 91 | 2,871 | 109 |

### Unsuccessful Bids to Host the Games

China has also tried to host the Games other times but was not chosen.

| Games | City | Winner of Bid |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [2000 Summer Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/2000_Summer_Olympics "2000 Summer Olympics") | Beijing | [Sydney](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sydney "Sydney"), Australia |
| [2010 Winter Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/2010_Winter_Olympics "2010 Winter Olympics") | [Harbin](https://kids.kiddle.co/Harbin "Harbin") | [Vancouver](https://kids.kiddle.co/Vancouver "Vancouver"), Canada |

## China's Olympic Journey

China has a rich history of participating in the Olympics. Let's look at how they've done over the years.

### Summer Olympics Highlights

China has won many medals in the Summer Olympics. They have especially excelled in certain sports.

*   **1984 Summer Olympics (Los Angeles):** China won 15 gold medals and ranked 4th. 
    *   Xu Haifeng won China's first-ever Olympic gold medal in **shooting**. This was a huge moment for the country.
    *   [Li Ning](https://kids.kiddle.co/Li_Ning "Li Ning") won six medals in **gymnastics** (3 golds, 2 silvers, 1 bronze). He was called the "Prince of Gymnasts."
    *   The Chinese women's volleyball team won China's first gold medal in a team ball sport.

*   **1988 Summer Olympics (Seoul):** China won 5 gold medals and ranked 11th. 
    *   Li Meisu won China's first medal in **athletics**.
    *   China also won its first medals in **rowing**.

*   **1992 Summer Olympics (Barcelona):** China won 16 gold medals and ranked 4th. 
    *   Chen Yueling won China's first **athletics** gold medal in women's 10 km walk.
    *   Chinese female swimmers won 4 golds and 5 silvers.
    *   [Deng Yaping](https://kids.kiddle.co/Deng_Yaping "Deng Yaping") won two **table tennis** golds. The IOC president himself gave her a medal.
    *   Zhuang Xiaoyan won China's first **judo** gold medal.

*   **1996 Summer Olympics (Atlanta):** China won 16 gold medals and ranked 4th again. 
    *   [Fu Mingxia](https://kids.kiddle.co/Fu_Mingxia "Fu Mingxia") won two **diving** golds, a rare achievement.
    *   [Deng Yaping](https://kids.kiddle.co/Deng_Yaping "Deng Yaping") won two more **table tennis** golds, becoming the first Chinese athlete to win four Olympic golds.
    *   China won all four gold medals in **table tennis** for the first time.
    *   The Chinese women's football team won a silver medal, China's first in **football**.

*   **2000 Summer Olympics (Sydney):** China won 28 gold medals and ranked 3rd. 
    *   China won all four gold medals in **table tennis** again.
    *   Chen Zhong won China's first **taekwondo** gold medal.
    *   Jiang Cuihua won China's first medal in **cycling**.

*   **2004 Summer Olympics (Athens):** China won 32 gold medals and ranked 2nd. 
    *   [Liu Xiang](https://kids.kiddle.co/Liu_Xiang_(hurdler) "Liu Xiang (hurdler)") became the first Chinese male athlete to win gold in an Olympic track event (110 m hurdles).
    *   Wang Yifu competed in his sixth Olympics and won gold in **shooting**.
    *   Meng Guanliang and Yang Wenjun won China's first **canoeing** gold medal.
    *   Li Ting and Sun Tiantian won China's first **tennis** gold medal.
    *   Wang Xu won China's first **wrestling** gold medal.
    *   The Chinese women's volleyball team won their second gold medal after 20 years.

*   **2008 Summer Olympics (Beijing):** As the host country, China won 48 golds, 22 silvers, and 30 bronze medals, totaling 100 medals, and ranked 1st. 
    *   [Guo Jingjing](https://kids.kiddle.co/Guo_Jingjing "Guo Jingjing") and [Zhang Yining](https://kids.kiddle.co/Zhang_Yining "Zhang Yining") both won two golds in **diving** and **table tennis**, respectively.
    *   China won all four gold medals in **table tennis** for the third time.
    *   Zhong Man won China's first men's **fencing** gold.
    *   Zhang Juanjuan won China's first **archery** gold.
    *   Zou Shiming and Zhang Xiaoping won China's first **boxing** golds.
    *   Yin Jian won China's first **sailing** gold in windsurfing.
    *   Chinese **gymnasts** won 11 golds, their best ever.

*   **2012 Summer Olympics (London):** China won 38 golds and finished 2nd. 
    *   Sun Yang became the first Chinese male swimmer to win Olympic gold.
    *   [Ye Shiwen](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ye_Shiwen "Ye Shiwen") became the first Chinese female swimmer to win two golds in one Olympics.
    *   [Chen Ding](https://kids.kiddle.co/Chen_Ding "Chen Ding") won gold in men's 20 km walk, China's second athletics gold.
    *   [Wu Minxia](https://kids.kiddle.co/Wu_Minxia "Wu Minxia") became the only Chinese athlete to win three gold medals in a single diving event.
    *   [Zou Kai](https://kids.kiddle.co/Zou_Kai "Zou Kai") won two more golds in **gymnastics**, making him the Chinese athlete with the most Olympic golds (five).
    *   Xu Lijia won China's first gold medal in the **sailboat** event of **sailing**.
    *   [Lin Dan](https://kids.kiddle.co/Lin_Dan "Lin Dan") became the first athlete to defend the men's singles title in Olympic **badminton**.
    *   China won all four gold medals in **table tennis** for the fourth time. They also won all five golds in **badminton** for the first time.

*   **2016 Summer Olympics (Rio de Janeiro):** China won 26 golds and ranked 3rd. 
    *   Gong Jinjie and Zhong Tianshi won China's first **cycling** gold medal.
    *   Feng Shanshan won China's first **golf** medal.
    *   Dong Bin won China's first medal in Olympic **triple jump**.
    *   The Chinese women's volleyball team won a third gold medal.
    *   [Wu Minxia](https://kids.kiddle.co/Wu_Minxia "Wu Minxia") defended her Women's 3m Synchro event for the fourth time, becoming the most successful Chinese athlete ever with 5 golds, 1 silver, and 1 bronze.

*   **2020 Summer Olympics (Tokyo):** Held in August 2021, China won 38 gold, 32 silver, and 18 bronze medals, ranking 2nd. 
    *   Su Bingtian set a new Asian Record in the men's 100 m semi-final and became the first Chinese athlete to reach the 100 m final.
    *   Gong Lijiao won China's first gold medal in any **field events** (women's shot put).
    *   Liu Shiying won China's first gold medal in Olympic **javelin throw**.
    *   Lü Xiaojun became the oldest weightlifter champion in modern Olympics.
    *   The Chinese relay team won China's first medal in **athletic relays**.

*   **2024 Summer Olympics (Paris):** China won 40 gold, 27 silver, and 24 bronze medals, ranking 2nd. This was their best result since the 2008 Beijing Olympics. 
    *   Zheng Qinwen won China's first-ever gold in Olympic singles **tennis**.
    *   Deng Yawen won China's first gold medal in **women's BMX freestyle**.
    *   Pan Zhanle won China's first gold in men's 100 m freestyle, breaking records.
    *   The Chinese swimming relay team won China's first gold in the 4 x 100 m medley relay.
    *   Chinese boxers won multiple gold and silver medals, their best result in **boxing**.
    *   The Chinese **diving** team won all 8 gold medals.
    *   [Liu Qingyi](https://kids.kiddle.co/Liu_Qingyi "Liu Qingyi") won a bronze medal in **breaking**, a new Olympic event.
    *   The Chinese **artistic swimming** team won their first golds.
    *   The Chinese women's **field hockey** team won silver, their best result.
    *   The Chinese **table tennis** team won all five golds. [Ma Long](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ma_Long "Ma Long") won his sixth gold, becoming the Chinese Olympian with the most gold medals.

### Winter Olympics Highlights

China has won medals in 7 out of 15 Winter Olympics sports. Most of their gold medals come from **short track speed skating**.

*   **1992–1998:**
    *   Ye Qiaobo won China's first Winter Olympics medal in **speed skating**.
    *   Chen Lu won bronze medals in **figure skating** in 1994 and 1998.

*   **2002:**
    *   Yang Yang (A) won China's first Winter Olympics gold medal in **short track speed skating**.

*   **2006:**
    *   Han Xiaopeng became the first male athlete to win a Winter Olympics gold medal in **freestyle skiing**.

*   **2010:**
    *   Wang Meng won three golds in **short track speed skating**.
    *   Shen Xue and Zhao Hongbo won **figure skating** gold in pair skating after trying four times.

[Indonesia](https://kids.kiddle.co/Indonesia "Indonesia") first joined the [Olympic Games](https://kids.kiddle.co/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") in 1952. Since then, Indonesian athletes have competed in almost every [Summer Olympic Games](https://kids.kiddle.co/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games"). They missed only two Games: in 1964 and 1980. In 1964, they were banned because of a disagreement during the 1962 Asian Games. In 1980, they joined a boycott led by the U.S. The [National Olympic Committee](https://kids.kiddle.co/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") for Indonesia was formed in 1946 and officially recognized in 1952. Indonesia has never taken part in the [Winter Olympic Games](https://kids.kiddle.co/Winter_Olympic_Games "Winter Olympic Games"). This is because the country does not have many places for winter sports.

As of 2024, Indonesian athletes have won a total of 40 medals. Most of these medals, 22, are from [badminton](https://kids.kiddle.co/Badminton_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Badminton at the Summer Olympics"). They also won 16 medals in [weightlifting](https://kids.kiddle.co/Weightlifting_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Weightlifting at the Summer Olympics"), one in [archery](https://kids.kiddle.co/Archery_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Archery at the Summer Olympics"), and one in [sport climbing](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sport_climbing_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Sport climbing at the Summer Olympics"). Among countries in Southeast Asia, Indonesia is second in both gold medals (10) and total medals (40), right after [Thailand](https://kids.kiddle.co/Thailand_at_the_Olympics "Thailand at the Olympics").

Indonesia's first Olympic medal was a silver. It was won by archers Lilies Handayani, Nurfitriyana Saiman, and Kusuma Wardhani in the women's team event at the [1988 Seoul Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1988_Summer_Olympics "1988 Summer Olympics"). The country's first two gold medals came in 1992 at the [Barcelona Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/1992_Summer_Olympics "1992 Summer Olympics"). These were won by Susi Susanti and Alan Budikusuma in badminton singles. They later got married! The 1992 Games were also the first time Indonesia won more than one gold medal. Since then, Indonesia has won at least one gold medal at every Olympic Games, except for the [2012 London Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics").

In badminton, Indonesia is one of only two countries, along with [China](https://kids.kiddle.co/China_at_the_Olympics "China at the Olympics"), to have won gold medals in all five types of badminton events at the Olympics.

Indonesia's newest gold medalist is Rizki Juniansyah. He won the men's 73 kg weightlifting event in 2024. He even broke an Olympic record! At 21 years old, he became the youngest Indonesian to win an Olympic gold medal. He beat the record set by Susi Susanti in 1992. His gold medal came just hours after his teammate Veddriq Leonardo won the speed event in sport climbing. Both men were the first Indonesians to win Olympic gold medals in sports other than badminton. With two gold medals, the [2024 Paris Olympics](https://kids.kiddle.co/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics") was Indonesia's best Olympic performance since 1992.

**Xi Jinping** (born 15 June 1953) is a Chinese politician. He has been the top leader of China since 2012. This means he is the [General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party](https://kids.kiddle.co/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) and the chairman of China's military. Since 2013, Xi has also been the [President of China](https://kids.kiddle.co/President_of_China "President of China"). He is the first CCP leader born after the People's Republic of China was founded in 1949.

Xi's father was a Chinese communist leader. During the [Cultural Revolution](https://kids.kiddle.co/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution"), his father faced difficulties, and Xi was sent to live in a rural area. He lived in a cave house in Liangjiahe village. There, he joined the CCP and worked as a local leader. After studying [chemical engineering](https://kids.kiddle.co/Chemical_engineering "Chemical engineering") at [Tsinghua University](https://kids.kiddle.co/Tsinghua_University "Tsinghua University"), Xi began to rise in politics. He worked in coastal provinces like [Fujian](https://kids.kiddle.co/Fujian "Fujian") and [Zhejiang](https://kids.kiddle.co/Zhejiang "Zhejiang"). In 2007, he became a member of the CCP's top leadership group, the [Politburo Standing Committee](https://kids.kiddle.co/Politburo_Standing_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Politburo Standing Committee of the Chinese Communist Party"). In 2008, he became the [Vice President of China](https://kids.kiddle.co/Vice_President_of_China "Vice President of China"). He was seen as the next leader of China.

As China's leader, Xi has focused on making the country stronger. He started a big campaign against corruption. This campaign led to many officials being removed from their positions. He also introduced policies to help people become more prosperous and reduce poverty. He has supported state-owned businesses and focused on developing new technologies. During the COVID-19 pandemic, he led China's "zero-COVID" policy. This policy aimed to stop the virus from spreading.

In foreign policy, Xi has made China more assertive on the world stage. He has worked to expand China's influence globally, especially through projects like the [Belt and Road Initiative](https://kids.kiddle.co/Belt_and_Road_Initiative "Belt and Road Initiative"). He has also focused on China's relationships with countries like the United States and those in Asia. Under his leadership, China has increased its military strength.

Since Xi became leader, there have been changes in China's society. Censorship and mass surveillance have increased. There have also been concerns about human rights, especially regarding ethnic minorities. In 2018, China's constitution was changed to remove term limits for the president. This allowed Xi to serve more than two terms. His political ideas, known as Xi Jinping Thought, are now part of China's official documents. In October 2022, Xi began his third term as the CCP General Secretary. He was re-elected as president in March 2023.

## Early Life and Education

Xi Jinping was born in [Beijing](https://kids.kiddle.co/Beijing "Beijing") on 15 June 1953. He was the third child of [Xi Zhongxun](https://kids.kiddle.co/Xi_Zhongxun "Xi Zhongxun"), a well-known communist leader. His father held important jobs after the People's Republic of China was founded in 1949. Xi had two older sisters.

Xi attended schools in Beijing in the 1960s. In 1963, when he was ten, his father faced political difficulties. His father was sent to work in a factory. In 1966, the [Cultural Revolution](https://kids.kiddle.co/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution") began. This period stopped many students from going to school. Xi's family home was searched, and one of his sisters died due to the events of that time.

His mother was forced to speak against his father in public. His father was later put in prison in 1968. In 1968, Xi decided to leave Beijing for the countryside. On 13 January 1969, he arrived in Liangjiahe Village in [Shaanxi](https://kids.kiddle.co/Shaanxi "Shaanxi") province. This was part of a movement where young people were sent to rural areas. Life in Liangjiahe was very different from Beijing. Xi had to get used to many challenges, like dealing with fleas, finding enough food, and doing hard labor. This experience helped him understand the lives of poor farmers.

After a few months, he tried to return to Beijing but was arrested. He was sent to a work camp. He later went back to Liangjiahe. He became the local party secretary there. He lived in a yaodong, which is a type of cave house.

Xi spent seven years in the countryside. In 1973, he was assigned to another village to help with social education. He worked well with the villagers. He applied to join the Chinese Communist Party many times. His father's political problems made it difficult. But in early 1974, his application was finally approved. He then became the Party branch chairman of Liangjiahe.

After becoming a leader, Xi learned about [biogas](https://kids.kiddle.co/Biogas "Biogas") technology from another region. He brought this idea back to Liangjiahe. This helped solve fuel shortages in his village. He also led projects to dig wells for water, start small industries, and plant tobacco. In 1975, he was recommended for [Tsinghua University](https://kids.kiddle.co/Tsinghua_University "Tsinghua University"). From 1975 to 1979, he studied [chemical engineering](https://kids.kiddle.co/Chemical_engineering "Chemical engineering") there.

## Early Political Career

### Starting in Government

After graduating in 1979, Xi worked in government offices. He served as a secretary to Geng Biao, who was then the Minister of Defense.

### Working in Hebei

In 1982, Xi became a deputy party secretary in [Zhengding County](https://kids.kiddle.co/Zhengding_County "Zhengding County"), Hebei province. He worked with another leader to write a letter to the central government. They wanted to reduce the amount of crops farmers had to give to the government. Their efforts helped farmers earn more money.

As the party secretary of Zhengding County in 1983, Xi started many projects. He worked on developing local talents and building parks. He also helped restore a famous temple. He brought in a TV production company to film a show in Zhengding. This helped boost tourism and brought in a lot of money for the county. In 1985, Xi visited [Iowa](https://kids.kiddle.co/Iowa "Iowa"), USA, to learn about farming. After this trip, he was moved to Xiamen in Fujian province.

### Leadership in Fujian

Xi arrived in Xiamen in 1985. He helped create the city's first long-term development plan. He also worked on projects like preparing for Xiamen Airlines and improving roads. He married [Peng Liyuan](https://kids.kiddle.co/Peng_Liyuan "Peng Liyuan") while in Xiamen.

In 1988, he became the party secretary of Ningde. This area was not as developed as other parts of Fujian. Xi worked on reducing poverty and strengthening the local CCP. He wrote a book about his experiences there called _Getting out of Poverty_. In 1990, he became the Municipal Committee Secretary of [Fuzhou City](https://kids.kiddle.co/Fuzhou "Fuzhou").

The **President of China** is the official leader who represents the [People's Republic of China](https://kids.kiddle.co/China "China"). This role is mostly ceremonial, meaning it has many duties like a [head of state](https://kids.kiddle.co/Head_of_state "Head of state") but doesn't hold much real power on its own. However, since 1993, the person who is President also holds other very powerful positions. This includes being the leader of the [Chinese Communist Party](https://kids.kiddle.co/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) and the head of the military. This makes the President the _de facto_ (actual) top leader of China.

The President's job is part of China's unique government system, where the [National People's Congress](https://kids.kiddle.co/National_People%27s_Congress "National People's Congress") (NPC) is the highest power. The President works with the NPC's Standing Committee to do things a head of state would normally do in other countries. For example, the President can deal with international matters if the NPC Standing Committee agrees.

## History of the Presidency

### Early Beginnings

The idea of a state representative in China goes back to 1912. That's when [Sun Yat-sen](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sun_Yat-sen "Sun Yat-sen") became the first leader of the [Republic of China](https://kids.kiddle.co/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%931949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)"). The current form of the presidency started on October 1, 1949. It was first called the Chairman of the Central People's Government.

### The 1954 Constitution

In 1954, China created a new Constitution. This document officially set up the role of "state chairman." This chairman had some ceremonial powers, similar to today's President. The chairman also had military powers, leading the armed forces and the National Defence Council. They could also call special meetings with top government officials.

[Mao Zedong](https://kids.kiddle.co/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong"), a very important leader, was the first state chairman. He was elected in 1954.

### Changes and Abolition

In 1959, [Liu Shaoqi](https://kids.kiddle.co/Liu_Shaoqi "Liu Shaoqi") became the state chairman. He was re-elected in 1965. However, during the [Cultural Revolution](https://kids.kiddle.co/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution") in 1966, Liu Shaoqi lost his power. In 1968, he was officially removed from all his positions, including state chairman. This was against the Constitution, which said only the NPC could remove him. After Liu was removed, the position of state chairman was empty.

In 1975, China adopted a new Constitution that completely removed the state chairman position. The duties of representing the state were given to the chairman of the NPC Standing Committee instead. This change emphasized that the Communist Party was in charge of everything.

### The Presidency Returns in 1982

In 1982, the presidency was brought back with a new Constitution. Leaders decided it was important to have a President to represent the country. However, they wanted the President to have limited powers. The idea was for the President to be a symbolic figure, like a president in a country with a parliament. The real power was meant to be with the leader of the Communist Party, the Premier (head of government), and the head of the military.

At first, these top jobs were held by different people. But in 1993, [Jiang Zemin](https://kids.kiddle.co/Jiang_Zemin "Jiang Zemin") became President. He was already the leader of the Communist Party and the military. This made him the undisputed top leader of China. Since then, the President of China has also been the most powerful person in the Party and the military.

In 2018, a big change happened. The rule that limited the President to two terms was removed. This means the President can now serve for an unlimited number of terms. [Xi Jinping](https://kids.kiddle.co/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping"), the current President, explained this change was to match the presidency with his other powerful roles, which don't have term limits.

## How the President is Chosen

### Who Can Be President?

To become President, a person must:

*   Be a Chinese citizen.
*   Have the right to vote and be elected.
*   Be at least 45 years old.

### The Election Process

The President is chosen by the [National People's Congress](https://kids.kiddle.co/National_People%27s_Congress "National People's Congress") (NPC). The NPC's executive body, called the Presidium, suggests a candidate. In reality, the [Chinese Communist Party](https://kids.kiddle.co/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") decides who will be nominated. So far, only one candidate has ever been nominated for the presidency.

The NPC then votes to elect the President. They can also vote to remove the President from office. Both decisions are made by a majority vote. The President serves for five years, which is the same length as the NPC's term. Since 2018, the President must take an oath to the Constitution before starting their job.

## What the President Does

The President represents China both inside the country and to other nations. The Constitution says the presidency is a state body that performs state activities.

The President has several powers, but most of them need the approval of the [National People's Congress](https://kids.kiddle.co/National_People%27s_Congress "National People's Congress") (NPC). These powers include:

*   Announcing new laws.
*   Choosing and removing the Premier (head of government) and other ministers.
*   Granting pardons (forgiveness for crimes).
*   Declaring states of emergency.
*   Issuing orders for large-scale actions.
*   Giving out state awards.
*   Appointing and removing ambassadors to other countries.
*   Signing and canceling treaties with foreign countries.

One special power is conducting state visits to other countries. This is the only power that doesn't need NPC oversight. Because most presidential powers need NPC approval, the President is mainly a symbolic figure. They don't have direct control over how the government runs.

The President also suggests who should be the Premier. While the NPC confirms this choice, they have never rejected a nomination. The Premier is a very important job, so this power can give the President some influence.

## Line of Succession

If the President's office becomes empty, the [Vice President](https://kids.kiddle.co/Vice_President_of_China "Vice President of China") takes over. If both offices become empty, the chairman of the NPC Standing Committee temporarily acts as President. This continues until the NPC can elect a new President and Vice President.

The **monarchy of Thailand** is the [constitutional form of government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_monarchy "Constitutional monarchy") of [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand") (formerly _Siam_). The **king of Thailand** ([Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_language "Thai language"): พระมหากษัตริย์ไทย, [RTGS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Thai_General_System_of_Transcription "Royal Thai General System of Transcription"):_Phra Maha Kasat Thai_, pronounced[[pʰrá(ʔ)má.hǎː kà.sàt tʰāj]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Thai "Help:IPA/Thai"), historically the _king of Siam_; [Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_language "Thai language"): พระเจ้ากรุงสยาม, [RTGS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Thai_General_System_of_Transcription "Royal Thai General System of Transcription"):_Phrachao Krung Sayam_, pronounced[[pʰrá(ʔ).tɕâːw krūŋ sà.jǎːm]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Thai "Help:IPA/Thai")) is the [head of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_state "Head of state") and head of the ruling [Chakri dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chakri_dynasty "Chakri dynasty").

Although the current Chakri dynasty was founded in 1782, the existence of monarchy in Thailand is traditionally considered to have its roots in the founding of the [Sukhothai Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhothai_Kingdom "Sukhothai Kingdom") in 1238, with a brief [interregnum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interregnum "Interregnum") from the death of [Ekkathat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekkathat "Ekkathat") to the accession of [Taksin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taksin "Taksin") in the 18th century. The institution was transformed into a [constitutional monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_monarchy "Constitutional monarchy") in 1932 after the bloodless [Siamese Revolution of 1932](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siamese_Revolution_of_1932 "Siamese Revolution of 1932"). The monarchy's official ceremonial residence is the [Grand Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Palace "Grand Palace") in [Bangkok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangkok "Bangkok"), while the private residence has been at the [Dusit Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dusit_Palace "Dusit Palace"). The king of Thailand is [head of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_state "Head of state"), [Highest Commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highest_Commander_of_the_Royal_Thai_Armed_Forces "Highest Commander of the Royal Thai Armed Forces") of the [Royal Thai Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Thai_Armed_Forces "Royal Thai Armed Forces"), adherent of [Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism_in_Thailand "Buddhism in Thailand") and upholder of [religions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_Thailand "Religion in Thailand").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-1)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Monarchy_of_Thailand&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Origin

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Monarchy_of_Thailand&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origin")]

Further information: [Buddhist kingship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist_kingship "Buddhist kingship"), [Bhāruci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bh%C4%81ruci "Bhāruci"), [Chakravarti (Sanskrit term)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chakravarti_(Sanskrit_term) "Chakravarti (Sanskrit term)"), [Devaraja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devaraja "Devaraja"), [Mahāsammata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mah%C4%81sammata "Mahāsammata"), [Mandala (Southeast Asian political model)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandala_(Southeast_Asian_political_model) "Mandala (Southeast Asian political model)"), [Mandate of Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandate_of_Heaven "Mandate of Heaven"), and [Monarchy in ancient India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_in_ancient_India "Monarchy in ancient India")

Thai kingship evolved through 800 years of [autocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autocracy "Autocracy"). The first king of a unified [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand") was the founder of the [Sukhothai Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhothai_Kingdom "Sukhothai Kingdom"), King [Si Inthrathit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Si_Inthrathit "Si Inthrathit"), in 1238.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-JSS_014_1b_Coedes-2) This early kingship is said to be based on two concepts derived from [Hinduism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism "Hinduism") and [Theravada Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theravada_Buddhism "Theravada Buddhism") beliefs. The first concept is based on the ancient Indian _Kshatriya_ ([Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_language "Thai language"): กษัตริย์[RTGS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Thai_General_System_of_Transcription "Royal Thai General System of Transcription"):_Kasat_ pronounced[[kà.sàt]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Thai "Help:IPA/Thai")), or warrior-ruler, in which the king derives his powers from military might. The second is based on the Buddhist concept of _[Dhammaraja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dasavidha-r%C4%81jadhamma "Dasavidha-rājadhamma")_ ([Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_language "Thai language"): ธรรมราชา[RTGS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Thai_General_System_of_Transcription "Royal Thai General System of Transcription"):_Thammaracha_ pronounced[[tʰām.má.rāː.tɕʰāː]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Thai "Help:IPA/Thai")), Buddhism having been introduced to Thailand around the 6th century CE. The concept of the Dhammaraja (or kingship under Dharma) is that the king should rule his people justly, ethically, and in accordance with the [Dharma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharma_(Buddhism) "Dharma (Buddhism)") (Buddhist teachings).

These concepts were briefly replaced in 1279, when King [Ram Khamhaeng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ram_Khamhaeng "Ram Khamhaeng") ascended the throne. Ramkhamhaeng departed from tradition and created instead a concept of "[paternal rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paternal_rule "Paternal rule")" ([Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_language "Thai language"): พ่อปกครองลูก), in which the king governs his people as a father would govern his children.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-JSS_036_2b_PrinceDhani_Old-4) This is reinforced in the title and name of the king, as he is still known today, _[Pho Khun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pho\_Khun "Pho Khun") Ram Khamhaeng_ ([Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_language "Thai language"): พ่อขุนรามคำแหง)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-JSS_071_0g-5) meaning 'Father Ruler Ram Khamhaeng'. This lasted briefly. By the end of the kingdom, the two old concepts returned as symbolized by the change in the style of the kings: "Pho" was changed to "Phaya" or Lord.

### Kings of Ayutthaya

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Monarchy_of_Thailand&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Kings of Ayutthaya")]

Main articles: [Devaraja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devaraja "Devaraja"), [Chakravartin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chakravartin "Chakravartin"), and [Divine right of kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divine_right_of_kings "Divine right of kings")

See also: [History of Indian influence on Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Indian_influence_on_Southeast_Asia "History of Indian influence on Southeast Asia"), [Greater India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_India "Greater India"), [Indosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indosphere "Indosphere"), [Sanskritization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskritization "Sanskritization"), [Mandala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandala_(political_model) "Mandala (political model)"), and [Indianisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indianisation "Indianisation")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Birmanie_2._battle_betwenn_Burmese_and_Siamese_ok_fini_%2B.jpg/250px-Birmanie_2._battle_betwenn_Burmese_and_Siamese_ok_fini_%2B.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Birmanie_2._battle_betwenn_Burmese_and_Siamese_ok_fini_+.jpg)

King [Naresuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naresuan "Naresuan") of Ayutthaya fought several wars against the Burmese [Toungoo dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toungoo_dynasty "Toungoo dynasty") to preserve Siamese independence.

The Sukhothai Kingdom was supplanted by the [Ayutthaya Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayutthaya_Kingdom "Ayutthaya Kingdom"), which was founded in 1351 by King [Ramathibodhi I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uthong "Uthong"). During the Ayutthayan period, the concept of kingship changed. Due to ancient Khmer tradition in the region, the Hindu concept of kingship was applied to the status of the leader. Brahmins took charge in the [royal coronation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Thai_monarch "Coronation of the Thai monarch"). The king was treated as a [reincarnation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reincarnation "Reincarnation") of [Hindu gods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_gods "Hindu gods"). Ayutthaya historical documents show the official titles of the kings in great variation: [Indra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indra "Indra"), [Shiva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiva "Shiva") and [Vishnu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vishnu "Vishnu"), or [Rama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rama "Rama"). Seemingly, Rama was the most popular, as in "Ramathibodhi." However, Buddhist influence was also evident, as many times the king's title and "unofficial" name "Dhammaraja", the Pali form of the [Buddhist Dharmaraja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharmaraja_(Buddhism) "Dharmaraja (Buddhism)"). The two former concepts were re-established, with a third, older concept taking hold. This concept was called "[Devaraja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devaraja "Devaraja")" ([Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_language "Thai language"): เทวราชา) (or "divine king"), which was a concept adopted by the [Khmer Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmer_Empire "Khmer Empire") from the [Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms of Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java#Hindu%E2%80%93Buddhist_kingdoms_era "Java"), especially a scholar class based on Hindu [Brahmins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brahmins "Brahmins"). The concept centered on the belief that the king was an incarnation ([avatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avatar "Avatar")) of the god [Vishnu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vishnu "Vishnu") and that he was a [Bodhisattva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bodhisattva "Bodhisattva") (enlightened one), therefore basing his autocratic power on his religious, moral, and royal lineage.

The king, portrayed by state interests as a semi-divine figure, then became—through a rigid cultural implementation—an object of worship and veneration to his people. From then on the monarchy was largely removed from the people and continued under a system of absolute rule. Living in palaces designed after [Mount Meru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Meru "Mount Meru") ("home of the gods" in Hinduism), the kings turned themselves into a "[Chakravartin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chakravartin "Chakravartin")", where the king became an absolute and universal lord of his realm. Kings demanded that the universe be envisioned as [revolving around them](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandala_(political_model) "Mandala (political model)"), and expressed their powers through elaborate rituals and ceremonies. For four centuries these kings ruled Ayutthaya, presiding over some of the greatest period of cultural, economic, and military growth in [Thai history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Thailand "History of Thailand").

[Wat Phra Si Sanphet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Phra_Si_Sanphet "Wat Phra Si Sanphet") next to the king's palace was the most sacred Ayutthayan temple.

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Family_Tree_of_The_Kings_of_Siam.png/250px-Family_Tree_of_The_Kings_of_Siam.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Family_Tree_of_The_Kings_of_Siam.png)

Family tree of the Kings of Thailand

The Kings of Ayutthaya created many institutions to support their rule. Whereas [feudalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudalism "Feudalism") developed in the [European Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Middle_Ages "European Middle Ages"), Ayutthayan King [Trailokanat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trailokanat "Trailokanat") in the 15th century instituted _[sakdina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakdina "Sakdina")_, a system of social hierarchy which ranked the king's subjects according to the amount of land they were entitled to, according to their rank and position.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-JSS_057_1e-6)

_[Rachasap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachasap "Rachasap")_ is required by court etiquette as an [honorific register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_honorifics#Honorific_registers "Thai honorifics") consisting of a special vocabulary used exclusively for addressing the king, or for talking about royalty.

#### Royal authority

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Monarchy_of_Thailand&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Royal authority")]

The king was the established chief administrator, chief legislator, and chief judge, with all laws, orders, verdict and punishments theoretically originating from his person. The king's [sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign "Sovereign") was reflected in the titles "Lord of the Land" (พระเจ้าแผ่นดิน _Phra Chao Phaen Din_) and "Lord of Life" (เจ้าชีวิต _Chao Chiwit_). The king's powers and titles were seen by foreign observers as proof that the king was an [absolute monarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_monarchy "Absolute monarchy") in the European sense. However, in Siamese tradition, the duty and responsibility of the king was seen as developed from the [ancient Indian theories of royal authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_in_ancient_India#Authority_of_the_King "Monarchy in ancient India"), which resemble [enlightened absolutism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlightened_absolutism "Enlightened absolutism"), although the emphasis is not on [rationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationality "Rationality") but on [Dhamma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhamma "Dhamma").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-JSS_038_1c_LingatEvol-7) This was disrupted in 1767, when Thai digests of the [dhammasāt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhammasattha "Dhammasattha") (ธรรมศาสตร์) were lost when a [Burmese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burma "Burma") army under the [Konbaung dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konbaung_dynasty "Konbaung dynasty") invaded, sacked and burned the city of [Ayutthaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayutthaya_Kingdom#The_final_phase "Ayutthaya Kingdom").

### Kingdom restored

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Monarchy_of_Thailand&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Kingdom restored")]

An interlude filled by a short [civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taksin's_reunification_of_Siam "Taksin's reunification of Siam") was ended when [Taksin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taksin "Taksin") restored the country under what has been called the [Thonburi Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thonburi_Kingdom "Thonburi Kingdom"). Kingship during the Thonburi period saw the adoption of the 'personal kingship' system that was previously administered under [Naresuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naresuan "Naresuan") (but abandoned after his death). Taksin treated the concept of kingship by abandoning the shroud of mysticism usually adopted by many Ayutthayan monarchs; he often revealed himself to the common folk by partaking in public activities and traditional festivities. He did little to emphasize his new capital, [Thonburi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thonburi "Thonburi"), as the spiritual successor to Ayutthaya. He also emphasized the building of moats and defensive walls in Thonburi.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-8)

### Chakri kings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Monarchy_of_Thailand&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Chakri kings")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/King_Rama_I_of_Siam_%28Yodfa_Chulalok%29_Portrait.jpg/250px-King_Rama_I_of_Siam_%28Yodfa_Chulalok%29_Portrait.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_Rama_I_of_Siam_(Yodfa_Chulalok)_Portrait.jpg)

Thongduang, later King [Rama I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rama_I "Rama I") of Siam, founded the Chakri dynasty in 1782.

In 1782, [Phutthayotfa Chulalok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rama_I "Rama I") (Rama I) ascended the throne and moved the capital from the [Thonburi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thonburi "Thonburi") side to the (Krung Thep) [Bangkok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Bangkok "History of Bangkok") side of the [Chao Phraya River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chao_Phraya_River "Chao Phraya River"). There he established the [House of Chakri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Chakri "House of Chakri"), the current ruling dynasty of Thailand. (This first reign was later designated as that of Rama I in the list of [Rama Kings of Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rama_(Kings_of_Thailand) "Rama (Kings of Thailand)").) He also established the office of [Supreme Patriarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Patriarch_of_Thailand "Supreme Patriarch of Thailand") as the head of the [Sangha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangha_(Buddhism) "Sangha (Buddhism)"), the order of [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism "Buddhism")[monks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhikkhu "Bhikkhu").

During the [Rattanakosin period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rattanakosin_period "Rattanakosin period") the Chakri kings tried to continue the concepts of Ayutthayan kingship once again emphasizing the connection between the sovereign and his subjects. On the other hand, they continued to not relinquish any authority of the throne. Kings [Phutthaloetla Naphalai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rama_II "Rama II") (Rama II) and [Nangklao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rama_III "Rama III") (Rama III) created a semblance of a modern administration by creating a supreme council and appointing chief officers to help with the running of the government.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-Roberts-9)

[Mongkut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongkut "Mongkut") (Rama IV) marked a significant break in tradition when he spent the first 27 years of his adult life as a [Buddhist monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhikkhu "Bhikkhu") during which time he became proficient in the English language, before ascending the throne. As king, he continued the appointment of officers to his supreme council, the most notable being [Somdet Chao Phraya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somdet_Chao_Phraya_(title) "Somdet Chao Phraya (title)")[Prayurawongse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prayurawongse "Prayurawongse") and [Si Suriyawongse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Si_Suriyawongse "Si Suriyawongse"), both of whom acted as Chief Ministers for King Mongkut (and the latter as [regent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regent "Regent"), from the king's death in 1868 until 1873).

[Chulalongkorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chulalongkorn "Chulalongkorn") (Rama V) ascended the throne as a minor at age 15 in 1868, and assumed full duties on 16 November 1873. As a prince, he had been tutored in Western traditions by the [governess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governess "Governess"), [Anna Leonowens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Leonowens "Anna Leonowens").[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-10) Intent on reforming the monarchy along Western lines, during his minority he traveled extensively to observe western administrative methods. He transformed the monarchy along Western lines of an "[enlightened ruler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlightened_absolutism "Enlightened absolutism")". He abolished the practice of [prostration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chulalongkorn#Abolition_of_prostration "Chulalongkorn") in front of the monarch, and repealed many laws concerning the relationship between the monarch and his people, while continuing many of the ancient aspects and rituals of the old kingship.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-Wales-11) In 1874, he created a [privy council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_of_Thailand "Privy Council of Thailand") copied from the European tradition, to help him rule his Kingdom. During his reign Siam was pressured to relinquish control of its old tributaries of Laos and northern Malaya to Western powers, Siam itself narrowly avoided becoming a colony.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-JSS_082_0l_StuartFox_Conflict-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-JSS_082_0k_Meyers-13) In 1905, 37 years after his coronation, Chulalongkorn ended [slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery "Slavery") with the Slave Abolition Act. In 1867 slaves accounted for one-third of the Siamese population.

His son, [Vajiravudh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vajiravudh "Vajiravudh") (Rama VI), ascended to the throne in 1910 and continued his father's zeal for reform to bring the monarchy into the 20th century. The perceived slow pace of reform resulted in the [Palace Revolt of 1912](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_Revolt_of_1912 "Palace Revolt of 1912"). In 1914, Vajiravudh determined that the act providing for invoking [martial law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_law#Thailand "Martial law"), first promulgated by his father in 1907, was not consistent with modern [laws of war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laws_of_war "Laws of war"), nor convenient for the preservation of the security of the state, so it was amended to a more modern form that, with minor amendments, continued in force through subsequent changes in government.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-14)

[Prajadhipok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prajadhipok "Prajadhipok") (Rama VII) succeeded his brother in 1925. The [Eton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eton_College "Eton College") and [Sandhurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Military_Academy_Sandhurst "Royal Military Academy Sandhurst") educated monarch created a council similar to a [cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_(government) "Cabinet (government)"), where the most important government officials could meet to decide state affairs. This advisory and legislative council, styled the [Supreme Council of State of Siam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Council_of_State_of_Siam "Supreme Council of State of Siam") (Thai: อภิรัฐมนตรีสภา) was founded on 28 November 1925 and existed until 1932.

### Constitutional monarchy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Monarchy_of_Thailand&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Constitutional monarchy")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/King_Prajadhipok_Signs_Constitution_of_Siam_1932.jpg/250px-King_Prajadhipok_Signs_Constitution_of_Siam_1932.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:King_Prajadhipok_Signs_Constitution_of_Siam_1932.jpg)

[King Prajadhipok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prajadhipok "Prajadhipok") signing the [Constitution of Siam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Thailand#1932_constitution "Constitution of Thailand"), 10 December 1932.

In June 1932, a group of foreign-educated students and military men called "[the promoters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khana_Ratsadon "Khana Ratsadon")" carried out a bloodless [revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siamese_Revolution_of_1932 "Siamese Revolution of 1932"), seized power and demanded that King Prajadhipok grant the people of Siam a constitution. The king agreed and in December 1932 the people were granted [a constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Thailand "Constitution of Thailand"), ending 150 years of absolute Chakri rule. From then on the role of the monarch was relegated to that of a symbolic head of state. His powers from then on were exercised by a [prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Thailand "Prime Minister of Thailand") and the [national assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_of_Thailand "National Assembly of Thailand").

In 1935 Prajadhipok (Rama VII) abdicated the throne, following disagreements with the government. He lived in exile in the United Kingdom until his death in 1941. The king was replaced by his young nephew [Ananda Mahidol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ananda_Mahidol "Ananda Mahidol") (Rama VIII). The new king was 10 years old and was living abroad in [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland"). A council of regents was appointed in his place. During this period the roles and powers of the king were entirely usurped by the [fascist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascism "Fascism") government of [Plaek Phibunsongkhram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaek_Phibunsongkhram "Plaek Phibunsongkhram"), who changed the name of the kingdom from Siam to [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thaification "Thaification"), and aligned it on the side of the [Axis powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_powers "Axis powers") in the [Pacific theatre of World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_War "Pacific War"). By the end of the war Phibunsongkhram was removed and the young king returned. The [Free Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Thai "Free Thai") movement provided resistance against Japan during the war and helped rehabilitate Thailand after the war.

After Rama VIII's sudden death from a bullet wound in 1946, [Bhumibol Adulyadej](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhumibol_Adulyadej "Bhumibol Adulyadej") (Rama IX), aged 19 years old, became the new monarch. In establishing his rule, the king was aided by the efforts of the US government, who used the monarchy as a bulwark against communist gains in Southeast Asia.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-Rattanasengchanh-2012-15):50

King Bhumibol was one of the [world's longest-reigning monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest-reigning_monarchs "List of longest-reigning monarchs") at the time of his death on 13 October 2016, at the age of 88, having reigned for 70 years and 126 days.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-16)

### Contemporary monarchy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Monarchy_of_Thailand&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Contemporary monarchy")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/MahidolDay_at_SirirajHospital2018.jpg/250px-MahidolDay_at_SirirajHospital2018.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MahidolDay_at_SirirajHospital2018.jpg)

The king's image appears in every town and in many prominent locations

Since 2000, the role of the Thai monarchy has been increasingly challenged by scholars, students, media, observers and traditionalists, and as pro-democracy interests began to express their speech.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-18) Many deemed that a series of laws and measures relating to [lèse majesté in Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A8se_majest%C3%A9_in_Thailand "Lèse majesté in Thailand") are hindrances to freedom of expression. Dozens of arrests, hundreds of criminal investigations and multiple imprisonments have been made based on these laws.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-19) King Bhumibol Adulyadej's speech in his 2005 national birthday broadcast could have been interpreted as a suggestion that he [welcomed criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A8se_majest%C3%A9_in_Thailand#King_invites_criticism "Lèse majesté in Thailand").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-wrong-20)

The [lèse-majesté law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A8se_majest%C3%A9_in_Thailand "Lèse majesté in Thailand") is part of Thailand's criminal-law code and has been described as the "world's harshest lèse majesté law"[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-21) and "possibly the strictest criminal-defamation law anywhere".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-economist-22) Political scientist [Giles Ungpakorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giles_Ungpakorn "Giles Ungpakorn") noted that "the _lèse-majesté_ laws are not really designed to protect the institution of the monarchy. In the past, the laws have been used to protect governments and to shield military coups from lawful criticism. This whole [royal] image is created to bolster a conservative elite well beyond the walls of the palace."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-frenchmanjail-23) The Thai activist and magazine editor [Somyot Prueksakasemsuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somyot_Prueksakasemsuk "Somyot Prueksakasemsuk"), who was sentenced to eleven years' imprisonment for a violation of _lèse-majesté_ laws in 2013,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-24) is a designated [prisoner of conscience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_of_conscience "Prisoner of conscience") by Amnesty International.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-25)

The king is assisted in his work and duties by the Private Secretary to the King of Thailand and the [Privy Council of Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_of_Thailand "Privy Council of Thailand"), in consultation with the head of the cabinet, the [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Thailand "Prime Minister of Thailand"). In accordance with the country's constitution, the king is no longer the originator of all laws in the kingdom; that prerogative is entrusted to the [National Assembly of Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_of_Thailand "National Assembly of Thailand"). All bills passed by the legislature, however, require his royal assent to become law. The monarchy's household and finances are managed by the [Bureau of the Royal Household](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_the_Royal_Household "Bureau of the Royal Household") and the [Crown Property Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Property_Bureau "Crown Property Bureau") respectively, these agencies are not considered part of the Thai government and all personnel are appointed by the king.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-26)

The junta that took power in 2014 was aggressive in jailing critics of the monarchy.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-28) In 2015, it spent US$540 million, more than the budget of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, on a promotional campaign called "Worship, protect and uphold the monarchy." The campaign includes television commercials, seminars in schools and prisons, singing contests, and competitions to write stories and films praising the king. "This is not propaganda," [Prayut Chan-o-cha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prayut_Chan-o-cha "Prayut Chan-o-cha"), the leader of the junta, said. "The youth must be educated on what the king has done."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-NYT20150920-29)

In its [fiscal year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_year "Fiscal year") (FY) 2016 budget, the ruling military government has increased its expenditure for "upholding, protecting and preserving the monarchy" to 18 billion baht (US$514 million), an increase of 28 per cent for this budget line item since 2014 when it took power.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-30) Budget allocations to support the monarchy in FY2020 amount to 29.728 billion baht, or 0.93% of the total budget.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand#cite_note-31)
